papers.title: Biostimulant effects on winter wheat yield: a multi-site field study
papers.abstract: We tested a seaweed-derived biostimulant on winter wheat across six farms. Treated plots yielded more grain on average, with the effect varying by soil pH.
papers.full_text: Across 180 plots on six farms, the biostimulant increased mean grain yield by 0.28 t/ha (95% CI 0.12 to 0.44). The effect was larger on soils with pH below 6.5. We found no effect on grain protein. Effects of this size are agronomically relevant: at current prices 0.3 t/ha covers the product cost roughly three times. We recommend multi-site designs because single-farm trials over- or under-estimate the effect depending on local soil.

papers.title: NitroGrow: a nitrogen-use-efficiency biostimulant. Greenhouse evidence
papers.abstract: Greenhouse pot trials of the NitroGrow formulation showed improved nitrogen uptake in wheat seedlings under moderate nitrogen supply.
papers.full_text: In 96 pots, NitroGrow raised shoot nitrogen uptake by 11 percent at moderate nitrogen supply and had no effect at high supply. Greenhouse effects typically shrink in the field; we expect a field yield effect well below 10 percent. Field trials with pre-registered analysis plans are needed.

papers.title: Data-entry errors in agricultural field trials: frequency and consequences
papers.abstract: An audit of 40 field-trial datasets found that unit errors, duplicate rows and missing outcomes were common and often changed the study conclusion.
papers.full_text: We audited 40 datasets. 23 percent contained at least one unit error (most often kg/ha recorded as t/ha), 31 percent contained duplicated plot rows, and 45 percent had missing outcomes. In 6 of the 40 studies, correcting these errors reversed the statistical conclusion. A single kg/ha value in a t/ha column can inflate a treatment mean by orders of magnitude while still producing a nominally significant p-value because the variance also explodes. We recommend automated range checks, uniqueness checks on plot identifiers, and pre-registered exclusion rules.

papers.title: Welch's t-test should be the default for two-group comparisons
papers.abstract: Student's t-test assumes equal variances. Welch's version does not and loses little power when variances are equal. We argue it should be the default.
papers.full_text: Simulations across 10,000 scenarios show Welch's t-test controls the type I error rate when group variances differ, while Student's t-test can be badly miscalibrated with unequal group sizes. Report the mean difference with a confidence interval and an effect size, not only the p-value.

papers.title: Site-by-treatment interactions in on-farm fertilizer research
papers.abstract: Fertilizer responses varied substantially between farms. We show how to report site-level effects alongside the pooled estimate.
papers.full_text: Across 12 on-farm trials, the between-site standard deviation of the treatment effect was 0.15 t/ha, about half the mean effect. Pooled estimates remain useful, but authors should report site-level means and discuss heterogeneity as a limitation when the number of sites is small (fewer than 5).

papers.title: Replication of biostimulant trials: a coordinated multi-lab study
papers.abstract: Five independent labs repeated the same biostimulant protocol. Pooled effects were smaller than in the original single-site studies.
papers.full_text: The pooled effect across five labs was 0.21 t/ha, about 40 percent smaller than the original reports. Independent verification of the analysis pipeline caught two coding errors before publication. We recommend that a second team re-runs the analysis from raw data before submission.

papers.title: Economic thresholds for adopting yield-enhancing products in wheat
papers.abstract: We estimate the yield gain needed for biostimulants to pay off for wheat growers under typical European prices.
papers.full_text: With product and application costs of about 25 EUR/ha and wheat at 200 EUR/t, a gain of 0.125 t/ha breaks even. Gains around 0.3 t/ha give a return of roughly 2.4 to 1. Farmers adopt products when trials show consistent gains across sites.

papers.title: Reporting standards for agronomic field experiments (ARRIVE-Ag)
papers.abstract: A checklist for reporting field experiments: design, randomization, exclusions, primary analysis, effect sizes, and limitations.
papers.full_text: Minimum reporting items: randomization method; number of plots per arm; all exclusions with counts and reasons; the pre-registered primary analysis; effect estimate with 95% CI; secondary analyses labelled as such; and a limitations section.

papers.title: Soil pH moderates nitrogen biostimulant response
papers.abstract: Biostimulant response was strongest on slightly acidic soils and weak above pH 7.
papers.full_text: In a 3-year trial, the yield response to a nitrogen biostimulant fell from 0.42 t/ha at pH 6.0 to 0.08 t/ha at pH 7.2. Soil pH should be recorded and used as a covariate in secondary analyses.

papers.title: Large language model agents as research assistants: promise and pitfalls
papers.abstract: LLM agents can run analyses and draft papers, but they repeat data errors confidently unless an independent verification step is built in.
papers.full_text: In a benchmark of 50 analysis tasks with planted data errors, agents without a verification step reported the erroneous result 64 percent of the time. Adding an independent verifier agent that re-ran quality checks from raw data cut this to 8 percent.
